Experienced. Greek, “much abroad, shall abound with subtlety. (11.) I,” &c.
And. Greek, “And I know more than I announce.” (Grabe’s edition)
For. Greek, “On account of these things I have been saved:” (Haydock) by my great experience, which gives weight to my instructions.
From falling, or when a person is fallen.
Mockeries. Some Greek copies have “gifts.” Such unjust presents or sacrifices, God will abhor, Isaias xli. 8., and Deuteronomy xxiv. 15. (Calmet)
Bread. Greek, “a livelihood, killeth his neighbour; and he sheddeth blood, who keepeth back the hire of the workman.” (Haydock)
Labour? So, if your sacrifices be ill-gotten, they will not be received; and if you relapse, you will be as bad as ever. (Calmet)

Dead. Literally, “is baptized by or from the dead;” baptizatur a mortuo. (Haydock) — St. Cyprian thought this text was peremptory against the baptism of heretics; and the Donatists were of the same opinion. They seem not to have read, if he touch him again, which entirely alters the meaning. St. Augustine admonishes them of this; though he explains it of the pagan rather than of the Jewish purifications, to which it refers, Numbers xix. 11. See St. Augustine, contra Cres. i. 24., and ii. 25., and contra Petil. i. 9., and St. Cyprian, ep. ad Quint. (Calmet)
Prayer. A relapse makes the former repentance useless, Matthew xviii. 33. (Worthington)

Offerings. He cannot otherwise observe the law. (Haydock) — Virtue is the most acceptable sacrifice. (Calmet) — The sacrifices of penance, of justice, and of praise, are to be preferred before all external ones. (Worthington)

And to. Gr. (4.) "He," &c. (Haydock) — The peace-offering and that for sin, as well as the oblation of fine flour and of praise, (which is the most perfect of all) are noticed. (Calmet) — External sacrifice must not be neglected. (Worthington)
Sacrifice. Gr. adds, "of praise." (Haydock) — This was the true spirit of the law. (Calmet)

Lord. The poor, who present a virtuous heart, are more acceptable than the rich, who are buried in sin, though the latter may offer the most splendid sacrifices. (Haydock) — God requires that all should do according to their abilities. If they have nothing, they must fulfill the commandments, and he will be satisfied. Some have inferred from Ex. xxiii. 16. that the poor were rejected. But the meaning of the law is here explained. (Calmet)
Heart. Literally "mind." Gr. "eye," (Haydock) free from avarice. 2 Cor. ix. 7.
Sanctify: "set apart" for the use of the ministers, and of the temple. (Calmet) — God will reward thee much more. (Worthington)

Wicked; defective. Lev. xxii. 21. Mal. i. 7. Gr. "curtailed, or ill-acquired," (Calmet) or "do not bribe" God; ( dorokopei. Grot.) as the word is used 2 Mac. God will not regard our gifts, to let our offences escape punishment. Is. xlii. 1. (Calmet)
For, &c. is not in Greek. God will protect the defenceless. (Haydock)
He, or "it." (Calmet) — Prayer is personified, and presents itself before God.
Them, the Gentiles, &c. v. 23. Gr. "will not delay to punish them, till he crush the loins of the unmerciful. And," &c. (Haydock)
Unjust Egyptians, Syrians, and Greeks, who then oppressed the Jews.
Adam, who was not spared. (Calmet) — Gr. "of men and their desires." (Haydock) — Our version seems to be taken from the Hebrew (Du Hamel) — Adam sometimes denotes any man. (Menochius)
The. Gr. "mercy is beautiful," &c. Ps. ix. 10. (Haydock)

Have. He has pointed out the conditions for prayer, and now he gives a model. The Jews were at this time dispersed and subservient to the Egyptians or Syrians, which greatly afflicted them. (Calmet) — And shew. Greek, (2.) “send.”

That. Roman Greek omits the rest. But Grabe retains, “all nations which seek not after thee.” (Haydock) — This prayer implies a prediction of the Gentiles’ conversion, as the psalms do frequently in like terms, Psalm lxiv. (Worthington)
Sanctified, by chastising us, or by protecting our fathers in the desert.
End of our sufferings. The malice of our enemies is at the height.
Escapeth the sword, Deuteronomy xxxii. 36. He foretells the event, or wishes that they may be chastised, in order that they may enter into themselves, and adore the true God.
Other lord. The Syrian and Egyptian monarchs sometimes claimed divine honours, Daniel vii. 25., and xi. 36. (Calmet)
That. Greek transposes the rest, and has only, and thou, &c. (Haydock)
First-born. Exodus iv. 22. Wives, children, and servants, were called after their lord or father, Isaias iv. 1., and lxiii. 19., and Jeremias vii. 10.
Rest, where the temple is built, 2 Paralipomenon vi. 41., and Psalm cxxxi. 8.
Words, predictions, as heretofore; or with thy favours.
Thee. The Jews were more faithful after the captivity. The author seems to beg for the coming of the Messias.

People, which thou hast prescribed, Numbers vi. 24. (Calmet) — Direct. Greek, “All shall know.” — Art. Greek, “Lord art the God of ages.” (Haydock) — Here the prayer ends. (Calmet) — The author continues to instruct. (Haydock)

Another. Thus act discreetly in the pursuit of knowledge. The good may be distinguished from bad, as easily as venison can from other meats. (Calmet) — As there is a difference of meats, so must discretion be used in words, in the choice of a wife, &c. (Worthington)
Resist. Greek, “requite it,” as it deserves. (Haydock)
Man. Yet in marriage the temper of the person is to be considered.
More. Love is the most violent of all the passions, and nothing can afford greater content than a virtuous and consoling wife, chap. xxvi. 21. (Calmet)
Good, is not in Greek, but the context shews that it is necessary. (Haydock) — By concord small possessions increase, as by discord the greatest are lost. (Worthington)
Want. If he be not so at first, servants will soon ruin his affairs.
Rest, or abode with his wife and family. The Jews in general married, and such as delayed were deemed suspicious characters, Proverbs xxvii. 8. (Calmet)
Death. Greek explains this: (Calmet) I mean (2.) “a companion and friend turned?” &c. (Haydock) — True friendship is most necessary, and false most dangerous. (Worthington)
Death. Greek explains this: (Calmet) I mean (2.) “a companion and friend turned?” &c. (Haydock) — True friendship is most necessary, and false most dangerous. (Worthington)

Will. Grotius suspects that not is wanting. Yet, if such a false friend take up arms, it will only be (Calmet) for his own belly. (Menochius) — Not is ill-omitted in the Complutensian edition in the last part of the following verse.

Snare. Roman and Alexandrian Greek has at the end (Calmet) of ver. 11., “with him that suspecteth thee.” (Haydock)
